description.narrative:
Oxfam secured a fund from Oxfam Hong-Kong on climate and conflict for Tog-dheer region. The project principal objective is to enhance community cohesion and promote reciprocal resource sharing in the Togdheer region of Somalia contributing better management of resources and effective climate adaptation strategies to ensure more resilience to climate change. Project has two outcomes based on prior project assessment report undertaken by Candlelight whichj are namely: Outcome 1: Strengthened community cohesion and minimizedconflicts among diverse groups through the practice of reciprocal resource sharing and peacebuilding initiatives in Tog-dheer region. Outcome 2: Community members are equipped with climate-smart agricultural skills, have access to a disaster early warning system,enhanced veterinary services, and improved economic resilience to adapt to the adverse effects of climate change.
Project rationale Environmental challenges: Summer temperatures range from 30°C to 40°C, while cooler temperatures from December to February average20°C to 25°C. Rainfall is minimal and irregular, concentrated in the Gu (April to June) and Deyr (October to November) seasons, with annual averages of 200–300 mm. Soil is sandy to loamy with limited organic content, challenging agriculture. Natural vegetation includes shrubs, acacia trees, and hardy grass. Drought impact: frequent drought caused 80% livestock losses, crop failures, and drinking water shortages. Increasing water salinity has worsened potable water scarcity. Prolonged droughts have reduced household resilience, especially among the poor and vulnerable. HH incurred debts for food, farm inputs, and other needs, with many businesses goingbankrupt. Displacement and reliance on relatives and friends have increased. Farming plots and business sizes have been reduced Conflict induced inequality: Northern Togdheer faces conflicts with SSC Khatumo militia, threatening peace and community resilience. Spillovers from the Sool region's conflict are affecting nearby areas, making them military zones and hazard-prone. This conflict, combined with drought, is worsening community resilience. Livelihoods deterioration: The vast land in these locations is mainly suitable for herding sheep, goats, and camels, with cows limited to areas with good water access. Pastoralism remains the dominant livelihood, with emerging value chains around herding and livestock sales. This sector has cultural and historical significance beyond just livelihoods. Rain-fed farming focuses on grains, legumes, and fodder. Urban livelihoods are supported by small businesses providing essential goods and services. TOT linked the Urban-Rural FS. Casual labor, mainly for men, includes construction, carpentry, sand harvesting, and porting Clan rivalry and political manipulation: Clan-based conflicts over land and resources are intensified by climate-induced migration and competition. Recent conflicts in Cada Yurura and neighboring villages over access to water and grazing landhighlight the fragility of existing resource-sharing agreements Climate change, resource scarcity and conflict: Persistent drought,erratic rainfall patterns, and flash floods have created a reinforcing loop of resource scarcity and conflict. Limited water availability forces pastoralist and agro-pastoralist communities into direct competition for shared water points, often escalating into violent disputes. Degradation of grazing lands—caused by overgrazing, deforestation for charcoal, and soil erosion—reduces critical resources for livelihoods, further fueling disputes. These environmental stressors destabilize traditional systems of resource management, eroding trust and cooperation among communities
Project location: The project will be implemented in two districts of Burco and Odweyne, Tog-dheer region. Candlelight, Oxfam long term partner, is implementing the proect fully with close technical backstopping from Oxfam technical lead and Buro field team to ensure the pilot project is implemented according to plan. Beneficiaries: The project aims to reach 16,633 (F= 9978 and M=6652) people through conflict resolution activities. Beneficiaries include internally displaced individuals due to conflict and drought, host communities in Odweyne and Buro districts of Tog-dheer region, marginalized groups, female-headed families, households with elderly or disabled members, child-headed households, women of reproductive age, and persons with disabilities. The targeted beneficiaries include internally displaced individuals, marginalized groups, female-headed families, families with elderly and disabled members, child-headed households, women of reproductive age, and persons with The proposed climate and conflict proposal interventions aims to address the underlying causes of conflict via rehabilitation strategic grazing reserves, bringing different community for resource reciprocity and peaceful co-existence. This will be compounded with livelihoods restoration activities and reviving the natural resource base damaged due to relentless climatic hazards. In specific IDP sites, the project proposes to create income sources for people who do not have access to land. This will complement existing candlelight work.
Summary of Activities and total populations expected to be reached disaggregated by gender are as follows:
OUTCOME 1: Strengthened community cohesion and minimized conflicts among diverse groups including cross border communities through the practice of reciprocal resource sharing and peacebuilding initiatives in Tog-dheer region.
Output 1.1: Trained 100 traditional elders and community leaders in peacebuilding and conflict management, enabling them to mediate disputes effectively. Activity 1.1.1: Provide two-day training to 100 traditional elders and community leaders in peacebuilding, enabling them to facilitate at least 5 inter-community dialogues annually to address common challenges and build mutual understanding . The training will be conducted by the University of Hargeisa's Faculty of Peace and Conflict Studies. Through the program, participants will gain the skills to foster peaceful coexistence within communities and encourage collaboration among themselves to prevent the occurrence of conflicts. They will also be equipped with mediation techniques to help reconcile communities after conflicts and to restore peace and social bonds. Activity 1.1.2: A committee of seven individuals will conduct periodic evaluations within two designated districts or suites to ensure the peaceful and reciprocal sharing of natural resources and rangelands. They will supervise the implementation of harmonious resource-sharing practices among diverse groups and communities.
Output 1.2: Engage 2 stakeholders (e.g., community leaders, local officials, and Somaliland senate members resource managers) from various communities in a discussion organized by CHL on the governance and management of shared natural resources such as water and grazing lands Activity 1.2.1. Develop 10 community-level bylaws to ensure and define commitments, management, and utilization of resources. Bylaws function as community governance tools, outlining the use of natural resources,access rights, roles and responsibilities for rehabilitation, and the management of shared assets. Activity 1.2.2: Run awareness campaigns using local and social media to promote messages of peaceful coexistence and unity, link these messages to climate change awareness, and enhance visibility in the field. Activity 1.2.3. Train 20 community-based organizations in managing grazing land to strengthen natural resource management structures and promote fair utilization
OUTCOME 2: Community members are equipped with climate-smart agricultural skills, have access to a disaster early warning system, enhanced veterinary services, and improved economic resilience to adapt to the adverse effects of climate change.
Output 2.1 Early warning systems for 10 communities are advanced, ensuringimproved accessibility and effective dissemination Activity 2.1.1. Provide a one-week training program for 70 community-based earlywarning committee members across 10 target communities (with 7 members per village committee) to enable them to collect and disseminate early warning data within their localities. Each community based early warning committee will receive training on early warningdata collection, management and dissemination. These committees will be responsible in sharing data on early warning in their respective communities and will share with Somaliland’s responsible agency, NADFOR. Activity 2.1.2. Establish 10 community adaptation plans. Each community will develop a Climate Adaptation Plan (CAP) for resilience initiatives and preparedness measures. The committeeswill collaborate with the Somaliland Commission on early warning and disaster risk reduction and receive training from NADFOR to effectively serve as focal points. Output 2.2: Support 60 women affected by protracted drought and food insecurity with climate-smart agricultural training, farming tools, equipment and greenhouses. Activity 2.2.1: Provide climate-smart agriculture and rangeland management training, along with farm tools and seeds for 60 women. Activity 2.2.2: Supply 60 women with two greenhouses, including the cost of procurement, seeds, and two months of onsite training for the women groups managing them. Output 2.3: Establish three Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) groups, each with 20 women, in rural areas to promote business plan development and small business opportunities. Activity 2.3.1: Form three VSLA women's groups and provide business plan development training for 60 women. After the training, participants will create business plans for their VSLA groups to enhance their livelihoods. Output 2.4: Enhance the capacity and services of three veterinary drug shops in the target areas. Activity 2.4.1: Allocate US$1000 to each of the three veterinary drug shops to procure quality drugs. Coordinate with the Ministry of Livestock to provide services and ensure each shop receives sufficient kits to replenish up to 15 Community Animal Health Workers (CAHWs).

participating-org.narrative: Candle Light for Health and Education (CLHE) works in the Toghdeer region of Somalia and was founded in 1995. Its mandate is to contribute to setting up sustainable structures in education and healthcare. Its most important target group consists of women and other marginalised groups, such as returning refugees. CHLE is also working with former militia members and tries to integrate them in society. CLHE works closely with the local authorities, leaders and others. Its work includes formal and informaleducation, training,preventive healthcare, rehabilitating small school buildings, and small-scale income generating activities. CLHE also works on the environment. It is of the opinion that deforestation has a negative impact on cattle, which has negative consequences for people's health and nutrition. Not enough good grazing land and a lack of water increase people's mobility, disrupting education programs. Therelationship between Oxfam Novib and CLHE began in 1996. CLHE's organisation capacities havesince improved.
